title: A disabled theatre troupe makes the able-bodied the discriminated minority — and it isn't asking for your sympathy
dek: Yaoyao flips the whole social order: after a nuclear war most people are augmented, and the unaugmented able-bodied minority become the Sinners, the ones who have to fight for their rights. This isn't a lament — it's a power fantasy written for disabled people.
why: Mostly oral testimony, with no data or research framework; the value is in the concrete scenes and in how one play grew. Skip it if you want methodology and industry judgment.
who: People in public-interest work, theatre and community workshops; content people who want to understand why integration can't rest on goodwill alone; practitioners and volunteers in disability issues.
skip: The rehearsal clip at the start and the submission call-to-action at the end can be skipped.

points.h: Disabled women being unable to leave the house is the norm
points.body: Yaoyao's earliest work was the documentary Hanyā (寒鸦), about three disabled women's struggles with family education and employment. One of them, an older sister, had not left her home in 36 years; when her parents took her out to visit relatives at holidays, what she felt was ‘like being walked like a little dog or cat’. Later she got the first computer of her life, went online, and found a job as a telephone operator — no degree required, only a sweet voice. Once she had the job she bought herself a wheelchair and rolled out of the house. Another woman, a visually impaired mother, was allowed to breastfeed her baby for only five minutes before her mother-in-law took the child away, on the grounds that ‘you can't see, you can't raise a child’; for years afterward she fought her husband's family for custody. These testimonies made Yaoyao realise that being unable to leave the house was not an isolated case.

points.h: Disabled people's friends are all disabled people
points.body: A former colleague of Yaoyao's uses a wheelchair. When she moved, the only people she could ask for help were friends who also use wheelchairs, hauling load after load with bags hung all over the chairs. Yaoyao instinctively asked why she didn't call able-bodied friends who can walk upright — they'd have finished in half a day. The colleague paused, then said, I don't know any able-bodied people — she did not have a single able-bodied friend; even her friends all used wheelchairs. Yaoyao says she didn't know how to continue the conversation, and realised only one thing: if disabled and able-bodied people never even get the chance to meet, ‘you have no chance at integration at all’. That was the direct starting point for her later search for a drama teacher and her work in integrated theatre.

points.h: Writing the able-bodied as the discriminated Sinners
points.body: Leyi Theatre's first play, Reverse Future (逆转未来), does a straight identity reversal: a nuclear war turns most people disabled, and they become new humans through technological modification — electronic eyes, cochlear implants and the like; the remaining able-bodied minority, guilty of ‘the crime of starting the nuclear war’, become the Sinners, marginalised by society. Yaoyao's logic: since she herself is a situs inversus person, why not flip the whole society too, turning the rights disabled people now have to fight for into rights the able-bodied have to fight for — what she calls writing a power fantasy for disabled people. The core of the plot: a Sinner father, to spare his son from suffering for his able body, gets drunk, picks up a chainsaw and tries to cut off his son's legs, but ends up in a pool of blood himself; the son is charged with patricide, and the courtroom scenes open up the debate about Sinners and augmented humans.

points.h: How the unseen and the unheard partner up
points.body: Visually impaired actor Wang Xiaomin was pulled into a pairing by deaf actor Li Ning at an audition. His first reaction was blank: you can't hear, I can't see, how are we supposed to act. Li Ning's solution was to put his hand on the back of Wang's hand and trace, tapping once when it was Wang's line. Director Ma Yan says blind and deaf performers sharing a stage already exists abroad: the deaf person's hand rests on the visually impaired person's hand, and the visually impaired person can feel the movements. Wang Xiaomin says deaf people had been around him since childhood, but back then he saw them as two kinds of people born with a communication barrier, ‘absolutely impossible to communicate’, a barrier that was almost insurmountable — after this collaboration he and Li Ning became very good friends. The troupe also had to solve sign-language interpretation, real-time captioning on a big screen, and assigning a volunteer to each visually impaired actor for audio description.

points.h: Visually impaired actors cheat on stage with earphones
points.body: Only later in rehearsals did the director discover that the visually impaired actors were in fact ‘cheating’: they wore earphones, listened to their lines at several times normal speed, and delivered them live on stage without any trouble — the director had no way to assess it, and only wondered how the visually impaired actors got their lines down so fast. Conversely, the director doesn't know sign language, and could only watch everyone signing while laughing along, when in fact the actors might be complaining about him in sign. Once they got to know each other, everyone's little tricks became known.

points.h: She received the best production award from the ICU
points.body: In 2024, Reverse Future was selected for the Nanjing New Theatre Festival initiated by Stan Lai. That year Yaoyao's heart failed and she went into the ICU; the troupe nearly fell apart, and it was a friend who stepped in to gather everyone for rehearsals and take them to Nanjing. At the closing buffet, while the other groups' tables sat empty and their members dressed up waiting for the awards, only their table kept going back for more after finishing, thinking ‘how could it possibly be us’. In the end they won Best Production, the festival's highest award, and jury chairman Stan Lai stood and led the applause. The news reached the ICU at the same moment as the award, and Yaoyao lay in her hospital bed in tears. That October the play was invited to the Wuzhen Theatre Festival, the first integrated disability production, and the only one in the ‘Nothing Is Impossible’ section.

points.h: After writing this play, she changed her answer on being born
points.body: The second play, I Choose to Be Born (我选择出生), is set in a world where every country legislates that when a fetus reaches eight months, parents must use brainwaves to inform it of its health and family circumstances, and the fetus decides whether to be born. Among five families: deaf parents who must honestly tell their child you won't be able to hear either; a husband who deceives his wife into having a child; a family that favours boys over girls; and a final story adapted from Yaoyao's own experience. The troupe's actors couldn't get through the script, because their life experiences were eerily similar — only the conditions differed. Asked whether they would still choose to be born if they had it to do over, most of the troupe still said they would choose birth, because they still love this world; Yaoyao changed her answer: she used to say she would choose birth too, but now she might choose not to be born, because disabled people are forced to be born into this society, with no choice in the matter.

points.h: The same question, and Cai Cong answers it the opposite way
points.body: The episode sets the deaf couple in I Choose to Be Born against the real Cai Cong: Cai Cong and his wife are both visually impaired, and when his wife was pregnant many people urged them to get tests to see whether the child would inherit the visual impairment, but Cai Cong did not want to presume, merely because the child might also be visually impaired, that such a life was not worth starting — they believe they can give a child a loving family. The deaf couple in the play decide to let the child be born. Yaoyao and Cai Cong give very different answers, and the argument around this choice persists. The question the episode poses: when a family makes a choice, how much capacity to choose does it actually have.

quotes.text: She was taken aback too, and said, I don't know any able-bodied people. She didn't have a single able-bodied friend — even she and her friends all used wheelchairs.
I said, I'm a situs inversus person, so why don't we just flip the whole society too, and see what happens.
This play makes you think. The sincerity of the performance covers the flaws in its craft. And what's most striking is the troupe's refusal to be pitied.
None of us could get through it, because we felt our life experiences were eerily similar — only the conditions were different, but the experiences were the same.
I actually used to say I would choose to be born too, but if it were now, I might choose not to be born.
But perhaps what's really worth asking is: when a family makes a choice, how much capacity to choose does she actually have.
He was like a blade of grass in the wind, about to wither — but he was always growing.
